nodes.name: Gluteal muscles
nodes.layer: — (§1.2: a parent, neither drawn nor selectable; the TypeScript value follows the platform lane, the forearm's groups use 'mixed')
nodes.layerEvidence: Its three members span the surface (gluteus maximus), middle (gluteus medius) and deep (gluteus minimus) layers (kenhub.gluteus_medius, radiopaedia.gluteal_muscles); 'mixed' is the honest value if the type needs one.
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: The gluteus maximus is at the surface, the front part of the gluteus medius is covered only by fascia, and the gluteus minimus is deep (grays.gluteal_region, kenhub.gluteus_medius, radiopaedia.gluteal_muscles); the forearm marks its mixed-layer groups 'partial'.
nodes.databaseMuscleNote: The canonical list (shared/capabilityRank.ts) holds gluteus_maximus, gluteus_medius and gluteus_minimus separately, not the group.
nodes.location: The buttock and the outer side of the hip, from the back and side of the pelvis to the top of the thigh bone, in a surface, a middle and a deep layer.
nodes.whatItDoes: Straighten your hip, move your thigh out to the side and turn it, and hold your pelvis steady when you stand on one leg.
nodes.shapeNote: Together these muscles may make up most of the muscular outline of the buttock and the upper outer hip. Which muscle shapes which part of that outline cannot be read from the surface. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: A group, not a muscle: work is counted for the gluteus maximus, medius and minimus inside it.
Some references also count the tensor fasciae latae among the gluteal muscles; here it is listed on its own.
nodes.statusReason: Its function claim, hips:hips.gluteals.function, is reviewed. The evidence speaks of the gluteal muscles as a group (teachmeanatomy.gluteal_region, kenhub.gluteal_muscles), so the parent has a function claim; it has no node actions.

nodes.name: Gluteus maximus
nodes.layerEvidence: The broad, thick surface muscle forming the prominence of the buttock (grays.gluteal_region); shapes the superficial gluteal surface (kenhub.gluteal_muscles_video).
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: The surface muscle of the buttock, forming its prominence (grays.gluteal_region, kenhub.gluteal_muscles_video).
nodes.location: Back of the hip, at the surface: from the back of the pelvis, the sacrum and the tailbone, down and outward to the top of the thigh bone and the iliotibial band on the outer thigh.
nodes.whatItDoes: Straightens your hip, moving the thigh back or raising the trunk from a forward lean, and turns the thigh outward. Its upper fibres help move the thigh out to the side and its lower fibres help bring it in. It does most of its work when force is needed: rising from a chair, straightening up from a bend, climbing and running.
nodes.shapeNote: The surface muscle of the buttock, so it may contribute most of the buttock's muscular outline. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: Its upper and lower parts are counted as one muscle here. In one study the upper part was more active in exercises that move the thigh out to the side or turn it outward; that is short-term muscle activity, not growth.
Its outward turning is weaker with the hip bent, by one paper's reading of a cadaver study; it is counted for the hip held straight.
nodes.statusReason: Its function claim, hips:hips.gluteus_maximus.function, is reviewed.

nodes.name: Gluteus medius
nodes.layerEvidence: Only the back third lies under the gluteus maximus; the larger front part is covered by the deep fascia of the hip, the gluteal aponeurosis, not by muscle (kenhub.gluteus_medius; elsevier.gluteal_fascia; imaios.gluteal_aponeurosis). So the belly is in the middle layer and its front part reaches the surface beside the gluteus maximus, as §1.2 says. That the uncovered part lies 'above' the gluteus maximus is read from the coverage, not stated by the cited excerpts; a second-review search (SR23) described the uncovered part as the front and upper part of the muscle (Physiopedia, a wiki, read and not cited), which agrees.
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: Its larger front part is covered only by fascia, its back third by the gluteus maximus (kenhub.gluteus_medius, elsevier.gluteal_fascia).
nodes.location: Outer side of the hip, middle layer. Its back third lies under the gluteus maximus; its larger front part, higher on the side of the hip, is covered only by a thick sheet of fascia.
nodes.whatItDoes: Moves your thigh out to the side and holds your pelvis steady when you stand on one leg. Its front fibres help turn the thigh inward and its back fibres help turn it outward.
nodes.shapeNote: Its front part is covered only by fascia, so it may contribute to the contour of the upper outer hip beside the gluteus maximus; the rest lies under the gluteus maximus. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: How hip muscles turn the thigh can change as the hip bends, so its turning actions are counted here only as help.
nodes.statusReason: Its function claim, hips:hips.gluteus_medius.function, is reviewed.

nodes.name: Gluteus minimus
nodes.layerEvidence: The smallest and deepest gluteal muscle, under the gluteus medius (radiopaedia.gluteal_muscles; statpearls.gluteus_minimus).
nodes.location: Outer side of the hip, deepest layer: under the gluteus medius, from the outer surface of the pelvis to the front of the bony point at the top of the thigh bone, with some fibres into the hip joint capsule.
nodes.whatItDoes: Moves your thigh out to the side with the gluteus medius, helps hold your pelvis steady on one leg, and helps keep the ball of the hip seated in its socket. Its front fibres help turn the thigh inward.
nodes.shapeNote: Deep, under the gluteus medius, so it has little or no contour of its own; it may add to the general fullness of the side of the hip. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: Which way it turns the thigh, and whether it helps bend the hip, depends on the hip's position and on which part of the muscle is working.
nodes.statusReason: Its function claim, hips:hips.gluteus_minimus.function, is reviewed.

nodes.name: Tensor fasciae latae
nodes.layerEvidence: The most superficial muscle of the front and outer thigh, lateral to the hip joint, immediately beneath the skin (kenhub.tensor_fasciae_latae).
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: Just under the skin and easy to feel (kenhub.tensor_fasciae_latae), but small and enclosed between two layers of the fascia lata; the forearm marks superficial muscles whose outline is not wholly distinct 'partial'. 'clear' would also be defensible; the anatomy lane may prefer it.
nodes.location: Outer side of the hip toward the front, just under the skin, about halfway between the bony point at the front of the pelvis and the bony point at the top of the thigh bone; it joins the iliotibial band, which runs down the outer thigh to below the knee.
nodes.whatItDoes: Helps bend your hip, move your thigh out to the side and turn it inward, working with the gluteal muscles, and helps keep the pelvis level when you walk. Through the iliotibial band it also reaches below the knee.
nodes.shapeNote: It lies just under the skin at the front and outer side of the hip, so it may contribute to the contour there. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: Anatomy references describe its hip actions as helping roles, alongside the gluteal muscles.
References disagree about what it does at the knee, so no knee action is counted for it here.
nodes.statusReason: Its function claim, hips:hips.tfl.function, is reviewed.

nodes.name: Piriformis
nodes.layerEvidence: Deep to the gluteus maximus (kenhub.piriformis); one of the deep group of the gluteal region (teachmeanatomy.gluteal_region).
nodes.databaseMuscleNote: No canonical name for the piriformis in shared/capabilityRank.ts; the database lane may add one or leave it null.
nodes.location: Deep in the buttock, under the gluteus maximus: from the sacrum outward to the top of the bony point at the top of the thigh bone.
nodes.whatItDoes: Turns your thigh outward when the hip is straight, and helps move it out to the side when the hip is bent. It also helps hold the ball of the hip in its socket.
nodes.shapeNote: Deep, under the gluteus maximus, so it has little or no contour of its own. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: Shown beside the hip muscles because of where it sits; hip specialization does not target it.
Some references say that with the hip bent far its pull reverses and it turns the thigh inward; a study in living adults did not find that. No inward turning is counted for it here.
The sciatic nerve passes below it in most people; in some, part or all of the nerve passes through or above it.
nodes.statusReason: Its function claim, hips:hips.piriformis.function, is reviewed.

nodes.name: Iliopsoas
nodes.layerEvidence: The psoas major arises from the lumbar vertebrae and the iliacus from the iliac fossa (statpearls.iliopsoas), both deep; below the groin the iliopsoas forms the outer part of the floor of the femoral triangle, whose roof is skin, superficial fascia and the fascia lata (teachmeanatomy.femoral_triangle). So the belly is deep with a near-surface window in the femoral triangle, as §1.2 says.
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: Deep in the abdomen and pelvis; only a short stretch lies under fascia and skin in the femoral triangle (teachmeanatomy.femoral_triangle), not as a separately visible outline.
nodes.location: Deep in the lower abdomen and at the front of the hip: the psoas major from the lumbar spine and the iliacus from the inner bowl of the pelvis end together on a small bony point near the top of the thigh bone. Just below the groin it forms the outer part of the floor of the femoral triangle, the hollow at the top of the front of the thigh.
nodes.whatItDoes: Bends your hip: it is the main muscle that brings the thigh forward and up. The psoas part also helps steady the lower spine.
nodes.shapeNote: Mostly deep inside the abdomen and pelvis, so it has little or no contour of its own; only a short stretch lies near the surface, in the hollow just below the groin. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: References disagree about whether, and which way, it turns the thigh, so no rotation is counted for it here.
Counted as one muscle here: the psoas major and the iliacus end together and both bend the hip, though in one study their activity differed in a leg raise.
nodes.statusReason: Its function claim, hips:hips.iliopsoas.function, is reviewed.

nodes.name: Adductor group
nodes.layer: — (§1.2: a parent, neither drawn nor selectable; the TypeScript value follows the platform lane, the forearm's groups use 'mixed')
nodes.layerEvidence: Members span the surface (adductor longus, pectineus, gracilis), the middle (adductor brevis) and the deepest front layer (adductor magnus) (kenhub.adductor_brevis_video, grays.medial_femoral_muscles); 'mixed' if the type needs one.
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: Some members are at the surface of the inner thigh, others under them (kenhub.adductor_brevis_video, grays.medial_femoral_muscles, teachmeanatomy.femoral_triangle).
nodes.databaseMuscleNote: The canonical list holds adductor_magnus, adductor_longus, adductor_brevis and gracilis separately, not the group.
nodes.location: Inner side of the thigh, from the front and lower pelvis around the pubic bone down the inner side of the thigh bone, in layers from the surface to deep.
nodes.whatItDoes: Bring your thigh in toward the other leg and help steady the pelvis. The adductor magnus also helps straighten the hip.
nodes.shapeNote: Together these muscles may make up most of the inner thigh's fullness. Which muscle shapes which part of that outline cannot be read from the surface. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: A group, not a muscle: work is counted for the muscles inside it.
References differ on whether the pectineus belongs to the group; here it and the gracilis are listed in it, beside the three adductors.
nodes.statusReason: Its function claim, hips:hips.adductors.function, is reviewed. The evidence speaks of the adductors as a group (kenhub.hip_adductors, statpearls.adductor_strain), so the parent has a function claim; it has no node actions.

nodes.name: Adductor magnus
nodes.layerEvidence: From the front it lies behind the adductor brevis, which lies behind the pectineus and adductor longus (kenhub.adductor_brevis_video), so it is the deepest of the front's three layers; from behind, posterior dissection views of the most superficial muscles label it beside the semitendinosus and gracilis (anatomytool.ubc_posterior_lower_limb; stanford.bassett_182_6, with the fascia lata removed). That supports a back-view outcrop, seen only through image labels. One teaching page (learnmuscles, not cited) called it deep from both views. See deviation D1 on its layer relative to the adductor brevis. Second review: an independent search (SR22) found no written description of the back-view outcrop, and its summary called the muscle 'usually not visible' from behind (its own inference). Another (SR24) suggested a small front-view outcrop low on the inner thigh, from labelled images outside the standard's list. The back-view outcrop therefore rests on image labels alone; the anatomy lane should confirm it from an atlas plate before the drawing lane cuts it.
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: Mostly covered by the other adductors and the hamstrings; part of it is labelled among the most superficial muscles in posterior views (anatomytool.ubc_posterior_lower_limb, stanford.bassett_182_6).
nodes.location: Inner thigh, deepest of the adductors seen from the front: its adductor part runs from the pubic bone to the thigh bone, and its hamstring part from the sitting bone almost straight down to a bony point on the inner side of the thigh bone just above the knee. From behind, part of it lies on the inner side of the back of the thigh, beside the hamstrings and the gracilis.
nodes.whatItDoes: Brings your thigh in toward the other leg and straightens your hip: its hamstring part pulls the thigh back. It also helps steady the pelvis when you stand and walk.
nodes.shapeNote: Most of it lies under the other adductors and the hamstrings, so its own outline is only partly visible: it may contribute to the inner side of the back of the thigh and to the general fullness of the inner thigh. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: Its two parts are counted as one muscle here: the adductor part pulls the thigh in, the hamstring part also straightens the hip.
Its two parts are listed as turning the thigh in opposite directions, so no rotation is counted for it here.
nodes.statusReason: Its function claim, hips:hips.adductor_magnus.function, is reviewed.

nodes.name: Adductor longus
nodes.layerEvidence: The most superficial adductor (lecturio.medial_thigh_muscles); in the floor of the femoral triangle, whose roof is skin and fascia, its inner edge, by most accounts, forming the triangle's inner border (kenhub.adductor_longus, teachmeanatomy.femoral_triangle).
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: The most superficial adductor at the front of the inner thigh, under the fascia lata; its outline runs into the pectineus and gracilis beside it, which the forearm would mark 'partial'.
nodes.location: Front of the inner thigh, at the surface: from the front of the pubic bone, near the groin, down and outward to the middle of the back of the thigh bone. By most accounts its inner edge is the inner border of the femoral triangle.
nodes.whatItDoes: Brings your thigh in toward the other leg and helps bend the hip.
nodes.shapeNote: The most superficial adductor at the front of the inner thigh, so it may contribute to the contour of the upper inner thigh just below the groin. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: Whether it helps bend or straighten the hip depends on the hip's angle: in one computer model it bent the hip up to about 90 degrees of hip flexion and straightened it beyond that.
References disagree on which way it turns the thigh, and two studies found the direction changes with the hip's position, so no rotation is counted for it here.
nodes.statusReason: Its function claim, hips:hips.adductor_longus.function, is reviewed.

nodes.name: Adductor brevis
nodes.layerEvidence: Deep to the pectineus and adductor longus but superficial to the adductor magnus (kenhub.adductor_brevis_video; lecturio.medial_thigh_muscles). It is covered, so 'deep' fits a front view that has only a surface and a deep layer; but the sources put it above the adductor magnus, which §1.2 places on the middle layer. Deviation D1.
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: Covered by the pectineus and adductor longus (kenhub.adductor_brevis_video).
nodes.location: Upper inner thigh, under the pectineus and the adductor longus and in front of the adductor magnus: from the pubic bone to the upper part of the back of the thigh bone.
nodes.whatItDoes: Brings your thigh in toward the other leg and helps bend the hip.
nodes.shapeNote: Lies under the adductor longus and the pectineus, so it has little or no contour of its own; it may add to the general fullness of the upper inner thigh. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: References disagree on which way it turns the thigh, and one study found the direction changes with the hip's position, so no rotation is counted for it here.
nodes.statusReason: Its function claim, hips:hips.adductor_brevis.function, is reviewed.

nodes.name: Pectineus
nodes.layerEvidence: In the floor of the femoral triangle between the iliopsoas and the adductor longus, under a roof of skin and fascia (teachmeanatomy.femoral_triangle); not covered by another muscle.
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: Near the surface in the femoral triangle but flat and set between the iliopsoas and the adductor longus (teachmeanatomy.femoral_triangle; kenhub.pectineus), so no separate outline is expected.
nodes.databaseMuscleNote: No canonical name for the pectineus in shared/capabilityRank.ts.
nodes.location: Front of the upper inner thigh, just below the groin: a flat muscle from the upper edge of the pubic bone to the back of the thigh bone just below the hip, in the floor of the femoral triangle between the iliopsoas and the adductor longus.
nodes.whatItDoes: Bends your hip and brings your thigh in toward the other leg, and helps steady the pelvis when you walk.
nodes.shapeNote: Lies near the surface in the hollow below the groin, but it is flat and set between larger muscles, so it has little separately visible contour. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: Shown beside the hip muscles; hip specialization does not target it.
Its nerve supply can be mixed, which is why some references group it with the front of the thigh rather than the inner thigh.
nodes.statusReason: Its function claim, hips:hips.pectineus.function, is reviewed.

nodes.name: Gracilis
nodes.layerEvidence: The most superficial muscle on the inner side of the thigh (grays.medial_femoral_muscles; statpearls.gracilis: the most superficial muscle of the medial thigh).
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: At the surface along the inner thigh (grays.medial_femoral_muscles), but long and thin, so its own outline is only partly distinct.
nodes.location: Inner edge of the thigh, at the surface: a long, thin strap from the lower front of the pelvis near the pubic bone to the inner side of the shin bone just below the knee.
nodes.whatItDoes: Helps bring your thigh in toward the other leg, and bends the knee and turns the lower leg inward. It is the only adductor that crosses both the hip and the knee.
nodes.shapeNote: The most superficial muscle on the inner side of the thigh, but long and thin, so it may contribute to the inner edge of the thigh's contour rather than to its fullness. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: Shown beside the hip muscles; hip specialization does not target it.
Its knee actions belong to the knee and are not counted on this page.
nodes.statusReason: Its function claim, hips:hips.gracilis.function, is reviewed.

claims.statement: The gluteal muscles of the buttock are taught in two groups. A superficial group of large muscles, the gluteus maximus, medius and minimus with the tensor fasciae latae, extends the hip and moves the thigh out to the side; a deep group of smaller muscles, the piriformis among them, mainly turns the thigh outward. The gluteus medius also holds the pelvis steady when one leg is off the ground, and the gluteus minimus helps steady it in walking.

claims.statement: The gluteus maximus extends the hip and turns the thigh outward (external rotation). Its upper fibres help move the thigh out to the side and its lower fibres help bring it in. Anatomy references describe it as the main hip extensor when force is needed, as in rising from a chair, straightening up from a bend, climbing and running. In a cadaver study of the hip's rotators it had a large capacity for turning the thigh outward, and a later paper citing that study notes that this capacity is reduced when the hip is bent. Through the iliotibial band it helps support the straightened knee.

claims.statement: The gluteus medius is a main hip abductor: the whole muscle moves the thigh out to the side, assisted by the gluteus minimus and the tensor fasciae latae. When one foot is off the ground, in standing, walking or running, it holds the pelvis steady over the standing leg. Its front fibres help turn the thigh inward, having the better leverage for it; one reference adds that its back fibres help turn the thigh outward when the knee is straight. How hip muscles turn the thigh can change as the hip bends: a cadaver study of the gluteal muscles and the other hip rotators found the pull shifting toward turning the thigh inward with hip flexion in most of the muscle parts it measured.

claims.statement: The gluteus minimus, the smallest of the gluteal muscles, lies just under the gluteus medius and is mainly a hip abductor and stabiliser: with the gluteus medius it moves the thigh out to the side and helps hold the pelvis steady in walking. In a cadaver and model study it could also act as a hip flexor, or turn the thigh either way, depending on the thigh's position and which part was working, and by tightening the hip joint capsule it helps hold the head of the thigh bone in its socket.

claims.statement: The tensor fasciae latae works with the gluteal muscles in bending the hip, moving the thigh out to the side and turning it inward; anatomy references describe it as assisting in each, and one calls it a relatively weak abductor and inward rotator. It joins the iliotibial band, which carries its pull to the shin bone below the knee; references disagree about what it does at the knee.

claims.statement: The piriformis is one of the short muscles that turn the thigh outward. claims.statement: The adductor magnus has two parts. Its adductor part, from the pubic bone, adducts the thigh. Its hamstring part runs almost vertically from the sitting bone (ischial tuberosity) to a bony point on the inner side of the thigh bone just above the knee; it is supplied by the sciatic nerve and extends the hip as well as adducting it. In standing and walking the muscle helps steady the pelvis. In an imaging study of 15 young adults with the hip in a neutral position, the muscle's estimated capacity to extend the hip was more than twice its capacity to adduct it. One reference lists the adductor part as also helping bend the hip and turn the thigh outward, and the hamstring part as turning it inward; an older study likewise found its fibres to the shaft of the thigh bone turning the thigh outward and those to the bony point above the knee turning it inward.

sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q9, quoted excerpts; the full article is behind a registration wall): the TFL works with the gluteus maximus, medius and minimus in hip flexion, abduction and internal rotation; it assists the rectus femoris in hip flexion; it is an accessory knee flexor only beyond 30 degrees of knee flexion and acts through the iliotibial band in lateral rotation of the tibia; in gait it pulls the ilium down on the weight-bearing side so the other hip rises and the swinging leg clears the ground. sources.title: StatPearls: Anatomy, Bony Pelvis and Lower Limb, Iliopsoas Muscle
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q15, Q16): the iliopsoas musculotendinous unit (psoas major, psoas minor and iliacus) is the main hip flexor and helps with external rotation and with stabilising the hip and lumbar spine; the iliacus stabilises the pelvis and supports hip flexion in running; the psoas major stabilises the lumbar spine in sitting and the femoral head in the first 15 degrees of movement; the psoas major arises from the lumbar vertebrae and the iliacus from the iliac fossa, both inserting on the lesser trochanter; lumbar plexus (L1-L3 to the psoas; femoral nerve to the iliacus). One mirror version lists absence of the psoas minor, accessory slips and bifid or multiple tendinous insertions among its variants. Mirrors carried different update dates (8 Jun 2026 and 6 Apr 2026), so the wording may have changed between versions. Authors not shown.

sources.title: StatPearls: Anatomy, Bony Pelvis and Lower Limb, Thigh Adductor Magnus Muscle
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q19): the hamstring portion runs nearly vertically from the ischial tuberosity to the adductor tubercle on the medial femoral condyle; both portions adduct the thigh and the hamstring portion also extends it; both work in gait and control the pelvis for posture; the adductor portion is supplied by the posterior division of the obturator nerve and the hamstring segment by the tibial portion of the sciatic nerve; Takizawa et al. found dual innervation of the adductor segment in 10 cadavers; the adductor segment is described as most of the muscle. Title shown on a statpearls.com mirror. The summary said sources differ on the adductor portion's other actions (flexion, external rotation); not used. Authors not shown.

sources.title: StatPearls: Adductor Strain
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q25, Q29, Q51; PubMed 29630218): the adductor group (magnus, longus, brevis) primarily adducts the thigh; the adductor longus also provides some medial rotation; the adductor magnus, through its ischial tuberosity attachment, contributes to hip extension, adducts in open-chain movement and helps stabilise the pelvis and leg in the stance phase of gait; the longus is the most often injured. A June 2023 snapshot adds secondary roles in hip flexion and rotation; the current text (updated Dec 2025) was seen only in part. A clinical article, cited here for its anatomy section. Authors not shown.

sources.title: Beck, Sledge, Gautier, Dora and Ganz, The anatomy and function of the gluteus minimus muscle (Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery, British volume, 82-B(3):358-363, 2000)

Bibliographic details as given by the search summary; the DOI is the one in the journal URL. PubMed id not shown.

sources.title: Variation of rotation moment arms with hip flexion (Journal of Biomechanics 32(5):493-501, 1999)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q8, Q14, abstract): rotation moment arms of the gluteus maximus, medius and minimus, iliopsoas, piriformis, quadratus femoris and both obturators measured in four cadavers at 0, 20, 45, 60 and 90 degrees of hip flexion and compared with a computer model; internal-rotation moment arms grew, external-rotation arms shrank, or a muscle switched from external to internal rotation as the hip flexed, a trend seen in 15 of 18 muscle compartments; the gluteus maximus had the largest capacity for external rotation. The abstract does not say which compartments switched. Authors (usually cited as Delp, Hess, Hungerford and Jones) were not shown in the snippet; one later summary named Delp and colleagues. Studied in the context of cerebral palsy gait.

sources.title: Gottschalk, Kourosh and Leveau, The functional anatomy of tensor fasciae latae and gluteus medius and minimus (Journal of Anatomy 166:179-189, 1989)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q10, abstract via PubMed and PMC1256751): in the authors' model the tensor fasciae latae's primary function is balancing the weight of the body and the non-weight-bearing leg during walking; the gluteus medius acts in phases and stabilises the hip early in the gait cycle; the gluteus minimus is a primary hip stabiliser in mid and late stance. Whether the study used EMG was not shown.

sources.title: Selkowitz, Beneck and Powers, Which exercises target the gluteal muscles while minimizing activation of the tensor fascia lata? Electromyographic assessment using fine-wire electrodes (Journal of Orthopaedic and Sports Physical Therapy 43(2):54-64, 2013)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q39, Q40): controlled laboratory study, 20 healthy adults, fine-wire EMG of the gluteus medius, superior gluteus maximus and TFL in 11 exercises; both gluteal muscles were more active than the TFL in unilateral and bilateral bridging, quadruped hip extension, the clam, sidestepping and squatting; the gluteal-to-TFL activation index was highest for the clam, then the sidestep, the unilateral bridge and the quadruped exercises. Every figure came from secondary summaries of the abstract (an exercise-science blog, a chapter abstract mirror and a journal excerpt), not the PubMed page itself; the PubMed id was given by a summary and the PubMed URL did not appear as a result. DOI not shown. Acute activity, not growth. Second review (SR13): an independent search agreed on every figure and gave the sample (twenty healthy persons, which the first pass's excerpt did not show) and the DOI 10.2519/jospt.2013.4116.

sources.title: Selkowitz, Beneck and Powers, Comparison of electromyographic activity of the superior and inferior portions of the gluteus maximus muscle during common therapeutic exercises (Journal of Orthopaedic and Sports Physical Therapy 46(9):794-799, 2016)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q41, abstract): 20 healthy persons; fine-wire EMG of the superior and inferior gluteus maximus in 11 exercises; the superior portion had greater relative activity in the 5 exercises that included hip abduction or external rotation; in the other 6 the portions did not differ, and exercises that mainly extend the hip loaded both portions similarly. sources.title: Hu et al., Is the psoas a hip flexor in the active straight leg raise? (European Spine Journal 20(5):759-765, 2011)

Co-authors beyond Hu were not listed in the results (the query's Meijer and van Dieen were not confirmed). EMG only, no force.

sources.title: Takahashi, Tozawa, Kawama and Wakahara, Redefining muscular action: human adductor magnus is designed to act primarily for hip extension rather than adduction in living young individuals (Journal of Applied Physiology 138(4):1088-1099, 2025)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q21, Q22, abstract and secondary citations): diffusion tensor imaging in 15 young adults with the hip in neutral; the posterior and anterior-distal portions made up most of the muscle's volume and cross-sectional area and had longer moment arms for hip extension than for adduction, so the estimated potential torque was more than twice as large for extension as for adduction; that potential correlated with measured maximal hip-extension torque. Only a citation-index page appeared as a result, not the journal page; PubMed id not shown; the second review (SR9) found the issue and the DOI, 10.1152/japplphysiol.00600.2024. sources.title: Pressel and Lengsfeld, Functions of hip joint muscles (International Society of Biomechanics congress abstract, 2005)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q49, one quoted passage): 'There is agreement in the literature that M. adductor longus is an adductor of the hip. sources.title: Poutoglidou, Piagkou, Totlis, Tzika and Natsis, Sciatic Nerve Variants and the Piriformis Muscle: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis (Cureus 12(11):e11531, 2020)

sources.title: Tomaszewski and colleagues, Surgical anatomy of the sciatic nerve: a meta-analysis (Journal of Orthopaedic Research 34:1820-1827, 2016)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q47, one quoted passage): 45 studies and 7,068 lower limbs; the normal pattern, the nerve leaving the pelvis as one trunk below the piriformis, was the most common, followed by the pattern the paper calls Type B (what Type B is was not shown). sources.title: Maher, Morrison and Zang, Effect of hip position on hip rotator strength and action of the piriformis using dynamic ultrasound (World Physiotherapy congress proceeding, 2019)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q11, Q13, abstract): the reversal of the piriformis's action with hip flexion rests mainly on cadaveric studies and static imaging and computational models; the authors designed a dynamic ultrasound study of 25 healthy adults to test it. Second review (SR3, SR4): its results were then seen. Prone and seated 90/90 rotation were tested; the muscle shortened in outward and lengthened in inward rotation in every hip position, which the authors read as no reversal of action. Rotator strength was higher seated than prone. Title as given by the result URL; whether it was later published as a full paper was not found.

sources.title: Study abstract on the rotating function of the iliopsoas and the single-joint thigh adductors in different hip positions (indexed by OrthoBullets as 8928937)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q17, one summarised line): reports that the iliacus rotates the thigh inward in every position of flexion and extension or abduction and adduction of the hip. Second review (SR7, SR21): a thread-based device measured the rotating function of the iliopsoas and the single-joint thigh adductors in different hip positions. The psoas major, pectineus, adductor longus and adductor brevis could turn the thigh either way depending on the hip's position: flexion and abduction strengthened outward turning, extension and adduction inward turning. The adductor magnus's fibres to the linea aspera turned the thigh outward and those to the adductor tubercle inward. A summary called 8928937 the PubMed id, and one secondary article may attribute the work to Reimann and colleagues (1996); neither was confirmed, and another summary dated the work to the 1960s. Title, authors, year and journal are therefore not confirmed, and the title here is descriptive. The key keeps its first-pass slug.

disagreementsAndWording: Hip rotation and hip flexion. A cadaver and model study (pmid.10327003) found the pull of most hip muscle parts it measured shifting toward turning the thigh inward as the hip bends, but its abstract does not say which parts. Muscle by muscle the recorded evidence is: piriformis, outward with the hip straight and inward past about 60 degrees by one reference (others, uncited, say about 90), resting mainly on cadaver and model work, while a dynamic ultrasound study of 25 adults found no reversal (wcpt.piriformis_action; second review SR3, SR4); gluteus minimus, inward by its front fibres with the hip bent by one reference, either way depending on position and part in a cadaver model; gluteus medius, no muscle-specific evidence found (Q57), so its claim states only the general finding. The claims say this plainly and the node actions count only what holds with the hip straight, as help where the sources say help. Second review: the gluteus maximus's outward-turning capacity is reduced with the hip bent by a paper citing the 1999 study (pmc.damiano_hip_rotation), and an older thread-method study found the psoas major, pectineus, adductor longus and brevis turning the thigh either way depending on the hip's position (orthobullets.iliacus_rotation; SR21). A computer model (isb.adductor_longus_moment_arm) found the adductor longus turning it outward up to about 80 degrees of hip flexion and inward beyond. Each of those claims now says so; none of these rotations is counted.

Adductor longus and hip flexion: a flexor up to about 90 degrees of hip flexion and an extensor beyond in one computer model (isb.adductor_longus_moment_arm, Pressel and Lengsfeld). The second review found no second source for the angle; an uncited summary put the adductors' change between about 40 and 70 degrees (SR8). Said in the claim and a caveat; counted as assist for flexion only.

Adductor magnus and hip extension: Kenhub and StatPearls give extension to the hamstring part; StatPearls' adductor-strain article says the magnus 'contributes' to extension; an imaging study of 15 young adults estimated its extension capacity at more than twice its adduction capacity. Recorded prime on the first, second and fourth. The claim says what each found. Second review: the imaging estimate is for the hip in neutral (said in the claim now); a moment-arm source cited by a 2020 study gives the back part an extension moment (jbiomech.hip_adductor_stretch); how the extension leverage changes with hip flexion was seen only in secondary or uncited pages (SR8) and is not claimed.

Rotation by the adductors: adductor longus outward (Kenhub) versus some inward (StatPearls); adductor brevis outward (Kenhub) versus inward (Radiopaedia), with a Kenhub video calling it contested; pectineus possibly either way (Kenhub); and for the longus, brevis and pectineus an older study found the direction set by the hip's position (second review, SR21); adductor magnus parts listed in opposite directions (Kenhub). None counted; each claim says references disagree.

Iliopsoas rotation: StatPearls and Kenhub list it as helping turn the thigh outward; an older thread-method abstract reports the iliacus turning the thigh inward in every position tested and the psoas major either way by position (SR21). Not counted; the claim says the references do not agree.

Tensor fasciae latae at the knee: StatPearls an accessory knee flexor beyond 30 degrees with outward turning of the shin; Kenhub knee extension and outward turning. Not counted; the claim and a caveat say references disagree. Its hip actions are 'assists' in StatPearls and Elsevier and 'relatively weak' in Kenhub, which is why all its rows are assist.

Gluteus medius back fibres: StatPearls ties their outward turning to the knee being straight; Kenhub does not list outward turning at all. The claim says 'one reference adds … when the knee is straight' (the condition added by the second review).

Gluteus maximus and buttock shape: Wikipedia (read, not cited) says fat contributes much of the buttock's rounded shape; the shape notes carry the forearm's sentence that visible shape also depends on body fat, and no sentence says the muscle alone makes the outline.
Psoas minor: absent rates differ widely between studies and populations, and the two cited studies disagree on whether race matters. The variation claim states both without a figure.

Pectineus nerve supply: Kenhub gives the femoral nerve with the obturator as a variant; Radiopaedia splits the muscle between the femoral and accessory obturator nerves. The claim says 'described as mixed' and 'may supply'.

Pectineus nerve supply (second review): an independent search (SR26) found the femoral nerve the only supply in most people and an obturator or accessory obturator branch in a minority; the claim now says the femoral nerve supplies it and that the second supply is described by one reference and listed as a variant by another.

Adductor magnus back-view outcrop (second review): an independent search (SR22) found no written description of it; the image-label evidence is unchanged and the appearance claim now says only what the labels show.
productQuestions: TFL has no prime row on the evidence (all three of its hip actions are 'assists' or 'relatively weak'). regionContent.test.ts ('gives every muscle a main action, adjacent muscles aside') will fail for hips.tfl, a target muscle. Either the anatomy lane marks hip.abduction prime as a product choice and says so, or the test allows a target muscle with assist rows only. Not decided here. Second review (SR12): study flashcards built on a kinesiology textbook list the tensor fasciae latae among the primary hip flexors and primary hip abductors, and Kenhub calls it relatively weak. If the lane reads that textbook and it says so, a prime hip.flexion or hip.abduction row would rest on evidence rather than on a product choice; the flashcards themselves cannot be cited.

No muscle of the hips is prime for hip.internal_rotation on the recorded evidence (gluteus medius, gluteus minimus and TFL are all assist), so the page never names inward rotation as a missing main action. If it should, marking the gluteus minimus's row prime is the closest product choice (see that row's productNote).
The adductor magnus's hip.extension row is prime on the evidence; the thigh's external listing of the adductor magnus (§1.2) depends on it being prime.

The thigh lane may want to know that the gracilis bends the knee and turns the lower leg inward (statpearls.gracilis, kenhub.gracilis); the gracilis's home is the hips and it is not listed by the thigh.
The pectineus and the piriformis are adjacent; their prime rows do not drive suggestions (recommendations.ts reads prime rows of target muscles only).
layerAndOutcropChecks: Gluteus medius: intermediate with a surface outcrop above the gluteus maximus, supported (only the back third under the gluteus maximus; the front part under the gluteal aponeurosis).
